title: The Glory of God
lead: Kavod, literally "weight," is God's visible splendor and presence: the fire and cloud on Sinai, the glory that fills the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 40:34; 1 Kings 8:11), comes to the exiles in Babylon, leaves and returns in Ezekiel (1:28; 8:4; 10:18–19; 11:22–23; 43:1–5; 48:35), and is seen in the face of Christ (John 1:14; 2 Corinthians 4:6). The rabbis called God's dwelling presence the Shekhinah.

sections.b: God's glory appears in fire and cloud at Sinai (Exodus 24:16–17), fills the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35) and later Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:10–11). Isaiah hears the seraphim say the whole earth is full of it (Isaiah 6:3). Ezekiel sees the glory leave the temple before its fall (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:22–23) and return to a new temple (Ezekiel 43:1–5). Haggai promises a greater glory for the rebuilt house (Haggai 2:7–9). In the New Testament the glory shines around the shepherds (Luke 2:9), is seen in the Word made flesh (John 1:14) and at the transfiguration (Luke 9:32), and is reflected in believers who see "God's glory shining in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Corinthians 4:6). The new Jerusalem needs no sun, because God's glory lights it (Revelation 21:23).
sections.refs: Exodus 24:16–17; 1 Kings 8:10–11; Isaiah 6:3; Ezekiel 10:18–19; Ezekiel 43:1–5; Haggai 2:7–9; John 1:14; 2 Corinthians 3:18–4:6; Revelation 21:23

sections.b: Ezekiel sees the glory of the LORD by the Chebar canal in Babylonia, among the exiles, not in the temple (Ezekiel 1:28; 3:12; 3:23). The same glory is seen leaving the temple, in two steps (Ezekiel 10:18–19; 11:22–23), and returning from the east to a new temple (Ezekiel 43:1–5). The chapter 1 vision therefore comes before the departure: the God who leaves a doomed city has already come to the people who were taken away from it.
